📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run.
  • When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

We all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

Industry observers note that there are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

You may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

According to recent reports, helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

When life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

Recent findings suggest that as one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

How to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

Sources indicate that this type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

In a recent development, how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and promptly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

How to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

It has been revealed that this technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

In a recent development, alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

This technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

According to recent reports, how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

The lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Recent findings suggest that use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

It has been revealed that practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Industry observers note that many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

Industry observers note that when anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

It has been revealed that if you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

If you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

Industry observers note that in fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to swiftly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The autonomic nervous system regulates everything from heart rate to digestion. Abnormalities may contribute to ADHD and POTS symptoms.

In a recent development, you probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up. These essential functions are managed by the autonomic nervous system, the body’s complex operating system, which runs quietly in the background.

The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.

In a recent development, some studies suggest that autonomic nervous system abnormalities may contribute to ADHD symptoms like inattention and impulsiveness. Clinicians may notice and use these symptoms to diagnose ADHD, but the underlying cause might reflect atypical autonomic nervous system activity.

Recent findings suggest that postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is an atypical or malfunctioning state of the autonomic nervous system. People with ADHD and/or hypermobility appear to have a higher prevalence of POTS than do members of the general population. Symptoms include dizziness or fainting when standing up from a sitting or lying position due to sudden changes in blood pressure and heart rate.

[Read: ADHD’s Curious Connections to Chronic Inflammation and Dysautonomia].

In individuals with hypermobility, autonomic dysregulation may be caused by irritation of the nerves that are intermittently stretched due to lax ligaments at the craniocervical junction, where the brain and upper spine meet.

A tilt table test, which measures your heart rate and blood pressure as you change position, is the main way POTS is diagnosed. Other assessments include blood and urine tests and a measure of the autonomic nerves that control sweating.

[Read: Exploring the ADHD-Inflammation Link].

In a recent development, some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering. I asked myself as a psychologist, “What happened to kindness? When did we lose it?”.

In a recent development, I started to dig into the research. In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts. They tracked “lost” wallets to see if they were returned. They found that more people were helping strangers than was reported before the pandemic, which may be surprising.

Other social science studies found that measurably happier people live in areas where community members tend to donate more, volunteer their time, or help strangers. In other words, helping inspires more helping.

[Download: Get a Grip on Tough Emotions].

What explains this kindness-happiness connection? In short, giving or receiving kindness kickstarts a “helper’s high” in our brains.

Research demonstrates that acts of kindness engage certain brain networks that release good chemicals like an internal pharmacy:.

It has been revealed that the dopamine from a helper’s high is different from the endorphin hit associated with running, gaming, or gambling, which keeps you wanting more. The dopamine generated in a helper’s high continues to produce positive feelings over time. The release of these neurotransmitters is especially helpful for people with ADHD who may struggle with emotional control, motivation, and stress.

Sources indicate that studies have shown that volunteering, even for one hour a week, can reduce inflammatory and stress cortisol responses, and even increase longevity. Volunteering is also considered a preventative action for loneliness and depression. Teens who volunteer outside their homes are more resilient and less likely to become depressed, according to research.

In a recent development, helping people learn to be kind to themselves is my lifelong challenge as a clinical psychologist. We tend to prioritize other people’s needs over our own. But the research is clear on self-compassion: When you talk to yourself in a kinder way, or do kind things for yourself, you’re learning how to quiet that inner critic.

[Read: Self-Compassion: The Latest ADHD Treatment].

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, mentioned:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This stated, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, noted:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • In a recent development, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

Sources indicate that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

In a recent development, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

According to recent reports, that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings important for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

However, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

Recent findings suggest that sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

It has been revealed that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

According to recent reports, compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Industry observers note that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a upcoming job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

According to recent reports, the struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a new schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

Industry observers note that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A upcoming job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

“I don’t travel much,” says Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

Breaking: The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

In a recent development, psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. #162023. Industry News: How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

Industry News: How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind.
  • If you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone.
  • According to recent reports, developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind. But here’s the truth: self-love isn’t something you’re born knowing how to do. It’s something you learn. And like any meaningful practice, it takes time, intention, and a lot of patience.

If you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone. Many of us were never taught how to speak to ourselves with compassion, how to set boundaries that honor our needs, or how to practice everyday self-respect. That’s where this guide comes in—because it’s never too late to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

According to recent reports, developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered. It means learning to treat yourself the way you’d treat someone you care deeply about—with gentleness, understanding, and care. Whether you’re struggling with self-worth, navigating difficult emotions, or simply trying to reconnect with the real you, these seven steps offer a foundation for how to practice self-love in real, actionable ways.

From building self-awareness and setting healthy boundaries to practicing forgiveness and celebrating your wins, this guide is here to support your growth. Start small, stay consistent, and trust that loving yourself is not only possible—it’s one of the most empowering things you’ll ever do.

In a recent development, self-love is exactly how it sounds—it’s a love for yourself and having an interest in your own well-being and happiness. Loving yourself doesn’t mean being self-centered or selfish. It’s about forming a caring relationship with yourself, like getting to know a good friend.

According to recent reports, the idea of loving yourself isn’t just a ‘feel-good’ concept—it’s essential for mental health. Research shows that self-compassion is linked to lower stress, reduced anxiety, and even improved physical health. People who actively practice self-love tend to set better boundaries, build stronger relationships, and experience less burnout.

Self-love is notable because the relationship you have with yourself sets the tone for how you deal with every aspect of life: your bonds with others, the way you handle challenges, and how you celebrate joys. When you’re kind and understanding toward yourself, you’re better equipped to navigate life’s ups and downs.

But how do you start loving yourself? Where do you even begin? Self-love starts with understanding where you stand right now. Take a look at your current feelings toward your mental health, motivation, and overall well-being. Are you harsh with yourself when things don’t go as planned? Do you forget to celebrate your wins, especially the small ones? These little check-ins can pave the path to walking toward self-love.

Industry observers note that loving yourself isn’t a switch you turn on or off. It’s a practice that takes time, commitment, and, well, practice, to cultivate. For many of us, the idea of loving ourselves feels out of reach. That’s why it’s often helpful to break the concept of self-love down into its distinctive elements — including self-trust, self-compassion, and self-awareness.

This can make it easier to start developing a self-love practice that feels achievable and manageable. So instead of viewing self-love as something you have to win at, try practicing these seven steps.

Self-awareness: Understand your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors.

Self-expression: Be true to who you are in all areas of life.

Self-care: Take care of your body and mind.

Self-trust: Believe in your ability to handle life’s ups and downs.

Self-compassion: Be kind to yourself, especially when times are tough.

Self-respect: Honor your worth by setting healthy boundaries.

Self-acceptance: Embrace who you are, including the parts you don’t find perfect. Remember what we mentioned about perfection?

Sources indicate that sometimes practicing self-love means taking action or establishing boundaries to protect your mental health. Here are a few IRL examples of how you can practice self-love today.

Prioritize rest to recharge: Imagine you’ve had a long week, and instead of squeezing in one more task, you decide to turn off your devices and enjoy a full night’s sleep. Studies have shown that adequate rest improves mood, cognitive function, and emotional resilience​. By honoring your body’s need for recovery, you demonstrate that you value your well-being above productivity.

Sources indicate that say no to unhealthy relationships: Picture being invited to a gathering where you know that certain individuals drain your energy. Choosing to decline isn't selfish; it’s self-preservation. Healthy boundaries are key to having self-respect and healthy relationships. Saying no clears space for connections that truly nourish you​.

Industry observers note that practice forgiveness for yourself: Maybe you’ve made a mistake at work and feel embarrassed. Instead of spiraling into self-criticism, try acknowledging the error, learning from it, and moving on. Self-compassion may help reduce anxiety and create more resilience, helping you recover more effectively from setbacks​. Mistakes are normal, and it’s all about “failing up”.

Recent findings suggest that create moments of mindfulness amid the chaos: Let’s say your day is hectic, and stress feels overwhelming. This is the moment to pause for a brief grounding exercise (here’s one of our favorites). Maybe you focus on your breath or tune into your surroundings. These types of practice not only calm your nervous system but also remind you of your ability to care for yourself even in small, meaningful ways​.

According to recent reports, treat yourself with the same kindness you show others: When you reflect on a recent accomplishment—big or small—you choose to celebrate it instead of brushing it off. There are huge benefits to recognizing your personal achievements. Giving yourself a pat on the back may help boost self-esteem and even long-term happiness​.

Self-love can feel unfamiliar and challenging to some of us, particularly if we’ve got into a habit of being hard on ourselves. The steps above can help break down the idea of self-love into more manageable elements.

In a recent development, but what practical things can we do to cultivate practices like self-awareness and self-trust? We got you. For each of the self-love steps, we’re sharing tools, techniques and exercises you can use to help get you closer to loving yourself.

According to recent reports, building self-awareness helps cultivate self-love by giving you further insight into what makes you who you are on an emotional level. Begin by tuning into your thoughts and feelings.

It has been revealed that what makes you feel happy, sad, or excited? Then, take it a step further. What makes you feel overwhelmed, overjoyed, or anxious? Knowing yourself is the first step to loving yourself.

Practice mindfulness: Try mindfulness practices to stay present and understand your thoughts and feelings better.

Educate yourself: Empower yourself through education by reading books, attending workshops, or engaging in discussions that promote self-awareness, self-compassion, and self-love.

Sources indicate that schedule regular self-check-ins: Reflect on your feelings, goals, and progress. Write them down, and revisit them often.

Tune into yourself through meditation: Spend some quiet time meditating to help declutter your mind and tap into your desires.

Let go of what no longer serves you: Let go of old habits or relationships that no longer contribute to your growth or happiness. We know this practice can be difficult, but removing what no longer brings you joy makes space for the good to come in.

💙 If you want to learn to relate to your thoughts in a healthier way, press play on Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty.

Loving yourself also means giving yourself permission to express your thoughts and feelings both inwardly and outwardly. Express yourself honestly in your day-to-day life. Be true to who you are, whether you’re simply chatting with friends or making massive decisions at work.

Engage in creative expression: Whether it's drawing, writing, or any other form of creative expression, allowing your creativity to flow freely can become an act of self-love.

According to recent reports, discover upcoming hobbies: Explore new activities that bring you joy and allow you to express yourself. Have you always wanted to try your hand at a group sport or acting? Now’s the time to try.

Journaling: Write down your thoughts, feelings, and experiences daily, and don’t hold back. Expressing yourself through writing can be cathartic and a helpful step in falling back in love with who you are.

It has been revealed that spend quality time with yourself: Enjoy your own manufacturer by doing things that make you happy. There’s a difference between doing something alone and feeling lonely. Embracing solo time and solo outings to the movies, dinner, or even a cooking class can be empowering, and, believe it or not, ridiculously fun!

💙 Journaling can be a great way to process feelings and encourage self-love. Check out our five Calm Journals plus our Feelings Wheel to get you started.

Sources indicate that caring for your body and mind plays a major role in cultivating self-love. Simple acts like mindful eating, exercise, and making time to relax can make a big difference in your overall well-being.

Take breaks when you need them: Remember to rest — even a micro-break can refresh and rejuvenate you. Want to amp up your rest break a notch? Take it outside. Being in nature can naturally calm and refresh your mind and body.

Practice relaxation: Use techniques like deep breathing or yoga to relax your body and focus on your breath.

Nourish your body: Fuel your body with nourishing food that makes you feel good.

Prioritize sleep: Ensure you get enough good-quality sleep—it’s crucial for your well-being.

Connect with your body through movement: Move your body in a way that feels good for you. It could be dancing in your apartment to your favorite album, walking outside, or stretching from the comfort of your bed.

Sources indicate that ask for support when you need it: Reach out for help when you need it. Asking for support is a sign of strength.

💙 Move your body with some Mindful Movement thanks to the Daily Move.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to love yourself if you don’t trust yourself. Embracing self-trust is about understanding that you have the ability to make the correct decisions for your life. Even when things don’t go as planned, believing that you can learn and grow from the experience is an crucial step in building self-trust.

Set realistic expectations: Set achievable goals to build your sense of accomplishment and reinforce the belief you have in yourself to overcome.

Recent findings suggest that practice patience: Be patient with yourself as you uncover what self-love means to you. Trusting yourself takes time. Let it.

Monitor your negative self-talk: Pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Are you harsh or unforgiving? Do you speak about yourself poorly? Take note of how you speak to yourself and work to make it more positive and encouraging.

Make a list of things you’re proud of: Reflect on your achievements and the things that make you proud. Look back on them when you need a dose of inspiration, and remind yourself and believe that you can make yourself proud again and again.

💙 Check out our 7 Days of Self-Esteem series to build your self-acceptance and boost your inner strength.

Sources indicate that be kind to yourself. Always. Especially when life gets tough. Celebrate your wins, learn from life’s mishaps, and don’t be too hard on yourself when it all doesn’t go as planned. Having compassion for self means you deeply care about your well-being. And feelings of deep care often mean love.

Practice positive affirmations: Craft and repeat positive phrases daily to help drive away those pesky negative thoughts.

Develop a self-forgiveness practice: Forgive yourself for past mistakes or perceived shortcomings. You’re only human. Remember that.

Try a loving-kindness meditation: Practice loving-kindness meditation to cultivate love and kindness toward yourself and others.

Put your hand over your heart and breathe deeply: This simple gesture can bring comfort and a sense of self-compassion.

💙 Try Loving-Kindness Meditation as a guided practice with Tamara Levitt.

Respect yourself by setting boundaries to show yourself—and others—that your desires, wants, and needs matter. When we respect our boundaries and our wants, we’re showing ourselves love by prioritizing our needs.

According to recent reports, seek supportive communities: Surround yourself with supportive, loving, and understanding people who uplift you. The more you’re around people you respect and admire, the more you might begin to respect, admire, and love yourself.

Sources indicate that set boundaries: Give yourself permission to say no to things or people that drain your energy. Setting boundaries and sticking to them is an act of self-love, as it showcases to the world around you that you give yourself what you want and need.

Volunteer: Engage in volunteer work to connect with a sense of purpose and community. Volunteer to walk dogs at a local animal shelter or serve meals at a community kitchen. Giving back brings a deep sense of purpose and gratitude, and a way to give yourself love is to give love to others in need.

In a recent development, celebrate your progress and success: Celebrate your wins, big or small, as all victories are steps toward growth. You’d cheer for a friend’s achievement, regardless of its size, wouldn’t you? Show yourself the same love and kindness and become your own cheerleader.

According to recent reports, honor your commitments to yourself: When you make a promise to yourself, keep it. Honoring your promises to yourself can help to build self-respect, which, as we’ve learned, enhances self-love by showing yourself that you’re a priority.

💙 Learn even more about self-love with our Relationship with Self series.

It has been revealed that embrace yourself wholeheartedly. Every single inch. Even the parts you’d like to improve upon. You have nothing to gain by being hard on yourself, and everything to gain by being loving and accepting of yourself as you move along on your path in life.

When you accept yourself, you’re declaring the love you have for yourself, regardless of what happens. Think of self-acceptance as a loving embrace.

Learn to laugh with yourself: Embracing a light-hearted approach toward life and how you view yourself can help you meet those challenging moments with more ease and less friction.

It has been revealed that embrace where you are now: Appreciate the present moment. You’re here now. So, be here now and try to enjoy the journey.

In a recent development, make space for your emotions: Allow yourself to feel your emotions. Emotions are natural, but ignoring them can become detrimental to your well-being.

Recent findings suggest that drop the comparison: Avoid comparing yourself to others. You’re unique and have your own journey.

In a recent development, practice gratitude: Cultivate gratitude by acknowledging the qualities you appreciate about yourself and your life. This can shift your focus from what's lacking to what's abundant.

💙 If you’re looking to build a daily gratitude practice, check out the 7 Days of Gratitude.

Sources indicate that morning affirmations: Start your day with one self-loving statement (e.g., "I am enough"). This may reduce stress and boost confidence.

Set small self-care goals: Even five minutes of journaling or stretching may shift your mindset toward self-love.

Mirror work: Look in the mirror and say something kind about yourself. It might feel awkward at first, but it may build self-acceptance.

It has been revealed that limit self-criticism: Notice when you’re being hard on yourself. Pause and reframe it as if you were talking to a friend.

In a recent development, practice gratitude: Write down three things you appreciate about yourself daily. Gratitude is potentially linked to higher self-worth.

Self-love is essential in relationships because it provides the foundation for healthy, balanced, and meaningful connections. When you love yourself, you develop confidence and emotional stability, which allows you to communicate your needs and feelings openly without fear of judgment. This clarity helps you to form stronger communications and can also reduce misunderstandings. Self-love also empowers you to set and maintain healthy boundaries, ensuring that your relationships are built on mutual respect rather than people-pleasing or overextending yourself. (Learn how to stop being a people pleaser with these 10 tips.).

When you feel secure in your own worth, you can offer love freely without expecting others to validate you, and you’re better equipped to accept care from others because you believe you deserve it. Ultimately, self-love nurtures healthier, more fulfilling connections by allowing you to show up as your best self, while also creating space for others to do the same.

Starting on the path of self-love begins with self-awareness. Notice your thoughts, feelings and actions. Begin to recognize what makes you smile or what makes you feel uneasy. Once you have a better understanding of yourself, you can start taking steps toward treating yourself with more kindness and respect. Remember, it's a journey—there are no deadlines, and you don’t have to rush. And if you ever feel lost, you can always revisit the seven steps to gently reintroduce self-love practices.

Industry observers note that if you're struggling to love yourself, start by identifying the thoughts that hold you back. Are you constantly comparing yourself to others? Do you feel unworthy of kindness? Self-love begins with self-awareness. Explore these steps to start loving yourself today:.

Shift your internal dialogue: Notice when you're being self-critical and replace it with a more compassionate thought.

Prioritize self-care: Even small acts like deep breathing or a 10-minute walk can reinforce your self-worth.

Surround yourself with positivity: Reduce exposure to toxic relationships or social media comparisons.

Celebrate small wins: Even recognizing personal growth (no matter how small) strengthens self-love.

Sources indicate that struggling with self-love is a common human experience, so you're not alone. Sometimes, past experiences, societal expectations, or harsh self-judgment can create blocks on the path to self-love. It's vital to remember that overcoming these hurdles takes time and practice, but with patience and persistence, it can get easier. Engaging in self-compassion practices and seeking support when needed are great steps when you encounter these struggles.

Lack of self-love can show up in different ways. It could be in the form of constant self-criticism, ignoring your own needs, or having difficulty with accepting compliments. It might also appear as feeling undeserving of positive experiences or neglecting self-care. The good news is that recognizing these signs is the first step toward change. Once you see them, you can start taking steps to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Self-love habits are small, daily actions that nurture a loving relationship with yourself. They could be as simple as speaking kindly to yourself, taking breaks when needed, or engaging in activities that make you happy. Other self-love habits include practicing gratitude, spending time in nature, eating nourishing food, and exercising in a way that feels good to your body. The goal is to create habits that make you feel loved, respected, and cared for.

Loving yourself isn’t a switch you flip—it’s a process. If self-love feels out of reach, start small. Acknowledge your feelings without judgment, challenge negative self-talk, and practice one self-kindness daily. Maybe it’s treating yourself with the same patience you’d give a friend, or simply recognizing that you deserve happiness.

One simple trick is to ask yourself, “If my best friend was feeling this way, what would I tell them?”.

Recent findings suggest that often, we extend kindness to others more easily than to ourselves. Flip that perspective inward.

Sources indicate that the first step in learning how to love yourself is awareness—tuning into your thoughts, noticing how you speak to yourself, and identifying patterns of self-criticism. Once you're aware of your inner dialogue, you can begin to shift it with self-kindness, small acts of self-care, and daily affirmations. Remember: every loving thought counts.

In a recent development, the meaning of self love is caring for yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally with the same compassion you’d offer someone you love. It means honoring your needs, setting boundaries, and treating yourself with kindness—not just when things are going well, but especially when they aren’t.

ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Big Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Fresh Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

It has been revealed that in clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

“These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John mentioned. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

Industry observers note that many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

It has been revealed that “This raises a really important question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John mentioned. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

Sources indicate that the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John noted.

[Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

According to recent reports, in doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John said.

It has been revealed that john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she said.

For more on ADHD in midlife and beyond, watch the full webinar at additu.de/111726.

Eight furniture designs informed by life in Newly introduced York City

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in Latest York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.
  • New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.
  • The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in Latest York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in Latest York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in Latest York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through Upcoming York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

What Still Holds, by Bechara Maalouf.

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Find out more about What Still Holds ›.

Pax Upcoming Yorkea, by Massimiliano Malagò.

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in New York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Find out more about Pax Latest Yorkea ›.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in Latest York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

Find out more about NYC Series ›.

White Picket Chair, by Han Seungmin.

Latest York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

First mass-produced in China in the 1980s, the fences are often used in Asian communities around the boroughs, and Han challenged “the idyllic image of the ‘American Dream’ from an immigrant perspective” through the piece.

Find out more about White Picket Chair ›.

HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM, by Kim Mupungilaï.

Belgian interior designer Kim Mupungilaï was prompted to design this collection of wood and fibre furniture after a 2018 visit to New York that inspired her to explore her half-Belgian, half-Congolese roots.

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Find out more about HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM ›.

The City Block, by Micah Rosenblatt.

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to New York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

Recent findings suggest that “[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen. “It’s the forms that you would look out and see on your horizon via whatever time period you’re in.”.

Find out more about The City Block ›.

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai.

Comedian and actor Julio Torres worked with furniture tech giant Sabai to create his first furniture collection, All Other Passports, debuted during NYC design week 2026.

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to New York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›.

For The Future of the Past, by Rafael Prieto.

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

Find out more about For The Future of the Past ›.

Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a fresh study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a fresh study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

According to recent reports, study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings showed that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

Premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

It has been revealed that the relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents mentioned that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

“I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, said. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

It has been revealed that “I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” said ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

Industry observers note that “Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

The researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors remarked they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.
